q: What is an embedding and why use it instead of one-hot?
a: A learned dense vector for a discrete item. One-hot vectors are huge, sparse and all equally distant; embeddings are compact and place similar items close together, so the model can generalise across related items.
Static (Word2Vec, GloVe): one vector per word regardless of context, so "bank" is the same in "river bank" and "bank loan". Contextual (BERT, LLMs): the vector depends on the surrounding sentence.

q: What is negative sampling in Word2Vec?
a: Instead of a softmax over the whole vocabulary, train a binary classifier to distinguish real (word, context) pairs from a few randomly sampled fake pairs. Same idea as in-batch negatives for modern contrastive embedding training.

q: How do you decide how much of a pretrained model to fine-tune?
a: Depends on data size and similarity to pretraining data. Small and similar: freeze backbone, train head. Small and different: fine-tune top layers carefully. Large: fine-tune everything with a low learning rate. Use smaller LRs for pretrained layers, gradual unfreezing, early stopping; LoRA when compute or forgetting is a concern.

When fine-tuning on a new task overwrites knowledge from pretraining, so general performance drops. Mitigate with low learning rates, few epochs, freezing layers, mixing in general data, or parameter-efficient methods like LoRA.
